title: Professional Scrum Product Owner I (PSPO I)
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the Scrum Guide 2020 and Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas. Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: A newly formed Scrum Team is discussing who is accountable for maximizing the value of the product delivered by the team. Which accountability belongs to the Product Owner?
options: Maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team
Coaching the team on how to use Scrum effectively
Creating the Sprint Backlog and adapting it during the Sprint
Ensuring the organization's security policies are enforced
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide 2020 states the Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team. Coaching the team is the Scrum Master's accountability, and creating and adapting the Sprint Backlog belongs to the Developers.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: An organization proposes that a committee of five managers share the Product Owner duties so that all departments are represented. What is the most appropriate response?
options: The Developers should decide which committee member to follow each Sprint
The Product Owner must be one person, and the committee should instead make its needs known to that person
The committee is acceptable as long as one manager is nominated as chair
The Scrum Master should take the Product Owner role alongside the committee
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide is explicit that the Product Owner is one person, not a committee, so the Product Backlog has a single clear orderer. Groups can influence the Product Owner through discussion, but accountability cannot be shared across a committee.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: A Product Owner delegates the day-to-day ordering of the Product Backlog to a trusted business analyst. What happens to the Product Owner's accountability?
options: Accountability is shared jointly between the Product Owner and the analyst
Accountability passes to the Scrum Master as process guardian
The Product Owner remains accountable for effective Product Backlog management
Accountability transfers to the business analyst who does the ordering
items.explanation: Delegation is allowed, but the Scrum Guide states that the Product Owner remains accountable. The analyst may perform the work, yet the Product Owner still answers for effective Product Backlog management.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: During Sprint Planning the Developers ask the Product Owner to clarify the long-term target they are working toward. What should the Product Owner describe?
options: A fixed release date for every remaining Product Backlog item
The complete technical architecture the Developers must follow
The exact number of Sprints the product will need
The Product Goal, which is a description of a future state of the product that provides a target for the team to plan against
items.explanation: The Product Goal describes a future state of the product and serves as a target the Scrum Team plans against; it lives in the Product Backlog. Release dates, architecture, and Sprint counts are not the Product Goal.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: A Scrum Team is reviewing its artifacts and commitments. Where does the Product Goal reside, and what artifact does it commit to?
options: The Product Goal lives in the Product Backlog and is its commitment
The Product Goal lives in the Sprint Backlog and is its commitment
The Product Goal lives in the Increment and is its commitment
The Product Goal lives in a separate vision document owned by stakeholders
items.explanation: The three artifacts each have a commitment: the Product Backlog commits to the Product Goal, the Sprint Backlog to the Sprint Goal, and the Increment to the Definition of Done. The Product Goal is part of the Product Backlog.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: A Product Owner wants the team to pursue two product goals at the same time in order to satisfy two customer groups. What guidance does Scrum offer?
options: Let the stakeholders vote each Sprint on which goal to follow
Focus the team on one Product Goal at a time before moving to the next
Run both Product Goals in parallel to maximize value
Assign one Product Goal to each half of the Developers
items.explanation: The Product Goal provides a single objective that focuses the Scrum Team. The Scrum Guide frames it as the team's objective, and pursuing multiple goals at once dilutes focus and empiricism.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: The Product Owner has a clear product vision, but the Developers seem unsure why their Sprint work matters. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Ask the Scrum Master to write a technical specification
Increase the number of Daily Scrums to keep everyone aligned
Communicate the Product Goal and how the current work moves the product toward it
Add more detailed task assignments for each Developer
items.explanation: Keeping purpose visible is a core Product Owner responsibility; sharing the Product Goal connects daily work to the product's future state. Task assignment and more meetings do not create shared purpose.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: Who is accountable for developing and explicitly communicating the product's target described in the Product Goal?
options: The Scrum Master
The Developers
The Chief Product Officer of the organization
The Product Owner
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide assigns the Product Owner the accountability to develop and explicitly communicate the Product Goal. The Scrum Master serves the team's process, and the Developers build the product.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: A large organization has many groups with an interest in the product. How does the Scrum Guide describe the Product Owner's relationship to these stakeholders?
options: The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog
The Product Owner must ignore stakeholders who are not on the Scrum Team
The Product Owner must form a committee with one representative per stakeholder group
The Developers decide which stakeholder needs reach the Product Backlog
items.explanation: The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders and is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog. Stakeholders do not order the backlog directly; they influence it through the Product Owner.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: A senior executive repeatedly bypasses the Product Owner and instructs the Developers on which features to build next. What does Scrum require for the Product Owner to succeed?
options: The Product Owner should remove the executive from the stakeholder list
The organization must respect the Product Owner's decisions so the role can be effective
The Developers must obey the executive because seniority outranks the Product Owner
The Scrum Master must add the executive's requests to the Sprint Backlog
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide states that for the Product Owner to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions. Bypassing the Product Owner undermines a single, clear ordering of the Product Backlog.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: Which accountability does the Scrum Guide assign to the Product Owner in relation to the Product Backlog?
options: Estimating the size of every Product Backlog item
Deciding the technical design of each Increment
Effective Product Backlog management
Writing all acceptance tests for every item
items.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for effective Product Backlog management, including clearly expressing items and ordering them to best achieve goals. Sizing is done by the Developers, and design is a Developer matter.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: A marketing manager wants a new feature added to the Product Backlog immediately. What does Scrum say the manager must do?
options: Add the item directly to the Product Backlog on their own authority
Ask the Developers to insert the item into the Sprint Backlog
Escalate the request to the Scrum Master for a decision
Convince the Product Owner, who alone is accountable for the Product Backlog order
items.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog, so anyone wanting a change must convince the Product Owner. Direct changes by others would break the single, clear ordering the role provides.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: A stakeholder introduces the Product Owner as the person who assigns tasks and tracks the Developers' daily output. Is this accurate?
options: No, because the Product Owner focuses on value and the Product Backlog while Developers self-manage their work
Yes, because task assignment is the Product Owner's primary daily duty
Yes, because the Product Owner is also the team lead and reports on each Developer
No, because those duties belong to the Scrum Master rather than the Product Owner
items.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for value and the Product Backlog, not for assigning work. The Developers are self-managing, and tracking individual output is not an accountability of either role.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: An organization plans to appoint a Product Owner who sits outside the Scrum Team and only meets the team at quarterly reviews. What does the Scrum Guide indicate?
options: The Product Owner's location is irrelevant because the Product Backlog is self-explanatory
The Product Owner is part of the Scrum Team and should engage closely with the Developers
The Product Owner can sit outside the team as long as decisions are documented
The Product Owner should meet only when a release is being planned
items.explanation: The Scrum Team consists of the Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers, so the Product Owner is inside the team. Close, ongoing collaboration is needed because the Product Backlog is refined continuously.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: During a Sprint Review, which contribution should the Product Owner make?
options: Approve each Developer's individual performance for the Sprint
Decide the Definition of Done for the upcoming Sprint
Discuss progress made toward the Product Goal and explain which Product Backlog items were or were not completed
Present the only slides while the Developers remain silent
items.explanation: In the Sprint Review the Product Owner explains what has been accomplished and discusses progress toward the Product Goal. The event is a working session, not a one-person presentation or a performance review.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: According to the Scrum Guide, who is responsible for sizing the Product Backlog items?
options: The Product Owner, because they order the backlog
The Scrum Master, because they protect the process
The stakeholders, because they fund the product
The Developers who will perform the work
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide places the responsibility for sizing on the Developers who will do the work. The Product Owner may provide context, but the people doing the work estimate it.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: A Product Owner is deciding the order of two Product Backlog items that require the same effort. What should guide the ordering?
options: Which item best helps the Scrum Team achieve the Product Goal and delivers the most value
Which item the Developers find more technically interesting
Which item was requested by the most senior stakeholder
Which item has the longest description
items.explanation: The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog to maximize the value the product delivers and to best achieve the Product Goal. Technical interest, seniority, and text length are not value-based criteria.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: How does a well-defined Product Goal contribute to empirical decision-making?
options: It lets stakeholders direct the Developers each day
It gives the Scrum Team a clear target so inspection and adaptation are anchored to a shared outcome
It fixes the exact scope so that no adaptation is needed
It replaces the need for a Sprint Goal
items.explanation: Empiricism relies on a shared target for inspection and adaptation, and the Product Goal provides that long-term target. It does not freeze scope, replace the Sprint Goal, or give stakeholders control of daily work.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: Developers need clarification about a Product Backlog item during the Sprint. What is the most useful Product Owner behaviour?
options: Instruct the Scrum Master to answer on the Product Owner's behalf
Ask the Developers to pick the interpretation they prefer and move on
Be available to clarify the item with the Developers so they can continue working
Tell the Developers to wait until the next Sprint Review
items.explanation: Product Backlog items are clarified through ongoing collaboration, and the Product Owner is the source of clarity on their intent. Deferring to the Sprint Review or guessing risks building the wrong thing.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: A Product Owner must decide whether a feature is worth building. What best reflects how value should be judged?
options: By the number of lines of code the feature adds
By how many features ship in a release regardless of their impact
By the number of meetings held to discuss the feature
By the outcome the feature produces relative to the product's goals, not by the amount of code written
items.explanation: Value reflects the outcome a product produces toward its goals and customers' needs. Output measures such as code volume or feature counts do not necessarily deliver value.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Product Ownership Fundamentals

items.stem: A Product Owner must decide what the Developers should work on next. Which approach best reflects good Product Backlog management?
options: Order the items to maximize value and progress toward the Product Goal
Order the items alphabetically so they are easy to find
Order the items by the date they were first requested
Order the items by the size of each item, smallest first
items.explanation: Effective Product Backlog management means ordering items to best achieve the product's goals and maximize value. Alphabetical, chronological, or size-based ordering is not value-based.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: The Scrum Team is clarifying and breaking down Product Backlog items so they are ready for upcoming Sprints. How does Scrum describe this work?
options: An activity that happens only during Sprint Planning
Product Backlog refinement, an ongoing activity rather than a formal event
A mandatory meeting that must be scheduled once per Sprint
A task owned solely by the Product Owner
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide describes Product Backlog refinement as an ongoing activity to break down and further define items. It is not one of the formal events and involves the whole team as needed.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: During refinement, who should perform the estimating of Product Backlog items?
options: An external estimation consultancy
The Scrum Master in consultation with stakeholders
The Developers who will do the work
The Product Owner alone
items.explanation: The Developers who will perform the work are responsible for sizing. They are closest to the work and can best judge the effort involved.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: A stakeholder asks for a complete, frozen Product Backlog before development starts. What does Scrum say about the Product Backlog?
options: It must be fully defined and frozen before the first Sprint
It is written once by stakeholders and never changed
It should list every task the Developers will perform
It is an emergent, ordered list that evolves as understanding improves
items.explanation: The Product Backlog is emergent and evolves as the product and understanding of it grow. Freezing it up front conflicts with empiricism and continuous learning.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: Two teams are working on the same product and each keeps its own separate list of requested work. What does Scrum recommend?
options: Maintain a single Product Backlog as the single source of truth for the product
Let each team maintain an independent backlog for speed
Merge the lists only at the end of the project
Store the lists in the Sprint Backlogs instead
items.explanation: The Product Backlog is the single source of work for the product. Keeping separate lists fragments prioritisation and undermines a coherent product direction.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: A Product Owner is ordering the Product Backlog. Which item should generally rank highest?
options: The item that has waited longest in the backlog
The item that delivers the greatest value or reduces the most risk for the product
The item the Product Owner personally enjoys most
The item with the most detailed description
items.explanation: Ordering should maximize value and reduce risk so the team learns and delivers the most important outcomes early. Personal preference and length of waiting are not ordering criteria.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: A stakeholder asks the Product Owner to commit to a precise date for delivering fifty future features. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Refuse to discuss dates under any circumstances
Commit to the date and require the Developers to work overtime to meet it
Use past performance and available empirical evidence to forecast a range, while making clear it is a forecast
Promise the exact date because confidence inspires the team
items.explanation: Forecasts should be based on empirical evidence such as past delivery, and communicated honestly as forecasts rather than guarantees. False precision and mandated overtime both undermine trust and transparency.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: A Sprint has ended and the Increment does not yet meet the Definition of Done. Should the Product Owner release it?
options: Yes, because releasing early always delivers value
Yes, provided the Developers promise to finish it next Sprint
Only if the Scrum Master grants an exception
No, because work that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released
items.explanation: An Increment is only created when a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done. Releasing unfinished work violates the artifact's commitment and hides the true state of the product.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: A Product Owner is choosing metrics to understand whether the product is succeeding. Which focus best reflects value?
options: Outcome-oriented measures such as customer behaviour and goal achievement
The total count of story points completed by the Developers
The number of hours each Developer logs each day
The number of Product Backlog items closed
items.explanation: Value is judged by the outcomes a product creates, not by effort or output. Story points, hours, and items closed are activity measures that do not by themselves demonstrate value.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: A large Product Backlog item is too big to complete in one Sprint. What is the most appropriate Product Owner action?
options: Assign it to a separate team that can work on it indefinitely
Collaborate with the Developers to break it into smaller valuable items that can flow through Sprints
Keep it whole and let it roll over between Sprints until it is finished
Drop it because large items cannot be managed
items.explanation: Refinement includes breaking large items into smaller ones that can be delivered incrementally. Keeping an unmanageable item whole, discarding it, or parking it on another team all reduce flow and value.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: The Developers report that technical debt is slowing delivery. How should the Product Owner treat technical debt items?
options: Place them at the bottom of the backlog until all features are done
Reject them unless a stakeholder requests them in writing
Consider them when ordering the Product Backlog because they affect the product's ability to deliver value
Ignore them entirely because they are a Developer concern
items.explanation: Technical debt affects future delivery and product quality, so the Product Owner should weigh it when ordering the backlog. Treating it as invisible or permanently lowest priority accumulates risk and slows the team.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: Halfway through a Sprint, a new high-value opportunity appears. How can the Product Owner respond within Scrum?
options: Immediately swap the work by editing the Sprint Backlog directly
Cancel the Sprint without consulting anyone
Ignore the opportunity until the next Sprint Review
Collaborate with the Developers to understand the impact and consider adjusting scope while protecting the Sprint Goal
items.explanation: The Sprint Goal should not be compromised, but scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Developers. The Product Owner does not edit the Sprint Backlog and should not cancel a Sprint casually.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: According to the Scrum Guide, which attributes help describe the items on a Product Backlog?
options: Description, order, size, and value
Owner, deadline, budget, and priority score
Author, reviewer, approver, and version
Risk score, defect count, cost, and test coverage
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide notes that Product Backlog items have the attributes of a description, order, size, and value. The other lists are borrowed management fields, not the artifact's defining attributes.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: A Product Owner is preparing large features for an upcoming Sprint. Which activity best supports this?
options: Asking stakeholders to estimate the items instead of the Developers
Refining and splitting the items with the Developers so they are small enough to complete within a Sprint
Writing complete specifications for every item alone
Locking the items so they cannot change during the Sprint
items.explanation: Refinement prepares items by breaking them into smaller, clearer pieces with the Developers. Writing specifications alone, freezing items, or having stakeholders size them conflicts with collaboration and Developer-led sizing.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: What must be true before the Scrum Team considers a product increment ready to release?
options: The Product Owner has personally tested every line of code
Every stakeholder has signed off on the release
The increment meets the Scrum Team's Definition of Done
All originally planned scope for the quarter has shipped
items.explanation: The Definition of Done is the commitment of the Increment; only work that meets it can be released. Quarterly scope, personal testing by the Product Owner, and universal sign-off are not Scrum requirements.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: Two Product Backlog items have similar value, but one can be delivered much sooner. Which ordering principle applies?
options: Always prefer the item that takes the most effort
Always prefer the item that was requested first
Deliver both items simultaneously regardless of capacity
Prefer the item that can deliver value sooner when other factors are equal, to shorten the feedback loop
items.explanation: Earlier delivery of value shortens the feedback loop and lets the team learn sooner. Preferring effort, request order, or overloading the team does not maximize value.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: How much detail should Product Backlog items contain before Sprint Planning?
options: Enough detail for the Developers to understand and work with them, refined continuously rather than fully specified up front
Complete technical specifications for every item
At least ten acceptance criteria for each item
No detail at all, because Scrum discourages documentation
items.explanation: Items are refined to the level of detail needed for the team to work effectively, evolving over time. Demanding full specifications or a fixed number of criteria contradicts emergence, and Scrum does not forbid documentation.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: A Product Owner wants to forecast how many items the team may finish in the next three Sprints. What basis is most appropriate?
options: The number of items currently in the Product Backlog
The team's observed historical delivery data used as a range or probability
A single number declared by the Product Owner without data
The maximum number ever achieved by any team in the company
items.explanation: Forecasting in Scrum is empirical, drawing on what the team has actually delivered and expressing uncertainty as a range. Invented numbers or unrelated benchmarks are not evidence-based.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: A Product Owner is asked whether shipping more features proves that the product is more valuable. What is the best answer?
options: Yes, because velocity is the only measure of value
No, because value cannot be assessed in any way
No, because value comes from outcomes achieved rather than merely from the number of features shipped
Yes, because more features always mean more value
items.explanation: Value reflects the outcomes a product produces for customers and the organization, not feature counts. Value can be assessed through outcome measures even though it is not a single fixed number.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: The Developers ask the Product Owner which item to pull next, and two items appear equally valuable. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Ask the Developers to vote and follow the majority
Refuse to choose until every stakeholder agrees
Let both items remain at the same rank in the backlog
Make a clear decision, weighing factors such as risk and dependencies, so the team can proceed
items.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for the order and should make a decisive choice when items seem equal, considering risk and dependencies. Leaving ties unresolved or deferring to votes avoids the accountability.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Value and Product Backlog Management

items.stem: A Product Owner wants stakeholders to stay engaged with the product. Which approach best supports ongoing collaboration?
options: Involve stakeholders regularly, including in the Sprint Review, and use their feedback to inform the Product Backlog
Limit stakeholder contact to a single annual meeting
Share only finished releases with stakeholders
Ask the Scrum Master to handle all stakeholder communication
items.explanation: Ongoing stakeholder collaboration and feedback loops inform ordering and keep the product aligned with needs. Restricting contact or delegating all communication weakens the relationship.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: In the Sprint Review, stakeholders give feedback that changes the perceived value of upcoming work. What is the appropriate outcome?
options: The Scrum Master rejects feedback that arrives mid-Sprint
The Product Backlog may be adapted to reflect the new insights
The feedback is recorded, but the backlog must stay fixed
The Developers immediately stop the Sprint and re-plan
items.explanation: The Sprint Review exists to inspect the outcome and adapt the Product Backlog based on new insights. Feedback is not merely recorded, and it does not automatically stop the Sprint.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: A stakeholder demands a guarantee that a feature will be delivered by a certain date. How should the Product Owner manage this expectation?
options: Avoid the topic until the date passes
Tell the stakeholder that dates are irrelevant in Scrum
Explain that delivery is forecast empirically and share transparent progress data instead of guaranteeing outcomes
Guarantee the date to keep the stakeholder satisfied
items.explanation: Honest expectation management means presenting empirical forecasts and transparency rather than false guarantees. Avoiding the topic or dismissing dates damages trust.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: Who should be invited to the Sprint Review to enable meaningful inspection and adaptation?
options: Only the Scrum Team, with no external attendees
Only the organization's executives
Only the customers who have signed a contract
Stakeholders and other key participants the Scrum Team invites
items.explanation: The Sprint Review is a working session that includes stakeholders and others the team invites, so the Increment and future direction can be inspected and adapted together.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: The Developers are unsure which customer problem a new feature is meant to solve. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Clarify the customer need and how the feature is expected to create value
Tell the Developers to implement it exactly as written
Ask the customers to instruct the Developers directly
Defer the feature until the next product roadmap cycle
items.explanation: The Product Owner brings the customer and product perspective and should clarify the problem the feature addresses. Direct customer instruction to Developers bypasses the Product Owner and risks misalignment.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: Two stakeholders want conflicting features in the same Sprint. How should the Product Owner respond?
options: Let the two stakeholders negotiate directly with the Developers
Make the trade-off decision and communicate the rationale, keeping a single coherent order
Ask the Developers to implement whichever is easier first
Add both features and let the team decide under pressure
items.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for ordering and should decide trade-offs transparently. Pushing the conflict to the Developers or letting stakeholders bypass the role undermines the single product order.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: A Product Owner wants early evidence that the product is on the right track. Which approach best uses feedback loops?
options: Survey internal staff only after the final release
Collect feedback once per year at the annual planning meeting
Deliver small increments frequently and gather feedback from real users early
Wait until the full product is complete before seeking any feedback
items.explanation: Frequent delivery of small increments creates short feedback loops that reveal whether the product meets real needs. Waiting for completion or annual reviews delays learning and increases risk.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: A powerful stakeholder insists on giving daily instructions directly to the Developers. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Allow the direct instructions to continue to keep the stakeholder happy
Ask the Scrum Master to block the stakeholder from all meetings
Tell the Developers to ignore the stakeholder completely
Reinforce that product direction flows through the Product Owner and invite the stakeholder to share needs that can be ordered into the backlog
items.explanation: The Product Owner channels stakeholder input into a single ordered backlog, while direct daily instructions fragment direction. Excluding the stakeholder or dismissing them entirely damages the relationship and loses valuable input.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: Stakeholders trust the Product Owner more when the Product Backlog is visible and understood. Which behaviour best builds that trust?
options: Keep the Product Backlog transparent and explain ordering decisions and progress openly
Share only the items that are already complete
Keep the ordering rationale confidential to preserve flexibility
Change the ordering frequently without explanation
items.explanation: Transparency about the backlog and the reasoning behind ordering builds stakeholder trust and supports empiricism. Hiding rationale or changing order without explanation erodes confidence.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: A customer emails a Developer directly with a request for a new feature. What does Scrum suggest should happen?
options: The Scrum Master should delete the request as out of process
The request should be routed to the Product Owner, who can consider it for the Product Backlog
The Developer should build it immediately because the customer asked
The Developer should add it to the Sprint Backlog without discussion
items.explanation: Requests flow to the Product Owner, who is accountable for the Product Backlog order. Developers building or adding unsanctioned work breaks the single order and the Sprint Goal, while deleting a request loses valid input.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: How does Scrum treat the balance between customer collaboration and detailed contracts or specifications?
options: Contracts are forbidden in Scrum engagements
Customer collaboration matters only at project closure
Collaboration with customers is valued, with specifications kept as light as useful while still being clear
Detailed specifications should replace all customer conversation
items.explanation: Scrum and the Agile values favour customer collaboration while keeping documents light enough to be useful. Replacing collaboration with specifications, banning contracts, or deferring collaboration all misstate the balance.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: When should a Product Owner seek customer feedback?
options: Only at the end of the project
Only during formal quarterly reviews
Only after all budget has been spent
Continuously, using short feedback loops and frequent increments rather than only at defined checkpoints
items.explanation: Continuous, short feedback loops let the Product Owner adapt the backlog to real needs. Restricting feedback to rare checkpoints delays learning and reduces the product's ability to deliver value.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: A stakeholder proposes a specific solution to a customer problem. What should the Product Owner do first?
options: Understand the underlying problem and need before committing to the proposed solution
Add the proposed solution to the backlog immediately
Reject the proposal because solutions come only from the Developers
Forward the solution to the Developers to estimate
items.explanation: Understanding the problem and need first lets the team explore better solutions and avoids building the wrong thing. Committing to a solution prematurely or rejecting input outright forgoes that understanding.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: A Product Owner wants stakeholders to understand where the product is heading. What is the most effective action?
options: Let each stakeholder infer the direction from the backlog order
Communicate the Product Goal clearly and connect it to the product vision and backlog
Send a detailed technical specification to all stakeholders
Withhold direction until features are complete
items.explanation: Explicitly communicating the Product Goal aligns stakeholders and the Scrum Team around a shared target. Withholding direction or leaving inference to chance creates misalignment.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.stem: A stakeholder asks the Product Owner to commit to delivering a fixed scope by a fixed date. What is the most honest approach?
options: Reject any discussion of dates as unprofessional
Agree now and negotiate reductions later
Explain the trade-off between scope, date, and quality, and use empirical forecasting rather than a fixed-scope promise
Accept the fixed scope and date without conditions
items.explanation: Honest expectation management acknowledges trade-offs and relies on empirical forecasting. Fixed-scope promises and later renegotiation damage credibility and transparency.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Stakeholders and Customers

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: A Product Owner proposes extending a Sprint beyond one month to finish extra work. What does Scrum say about Sprint length?
options: Sprints may be any length the Product Owner chooses
Sprints should be extended whenever the scope is not complete
Sprint length should change each Sprint to match the workload
Sprints are fixed-length and limited to one month at most to keep a consistent cadence
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide fixes the Sprint at one month or less and keeps it consistent to create a regular cadence and limit risk. Extending a Sprint based on remaining work removes that rhythm and predictability.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: During Sprint Planning, whose responsibility is it to ensure that the attendees discuss the most important Product Backlog items?
options: The Product Owner
The Scrum Master
The most senior Developer
The invited stakeholders
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide states that the Product Owner ensures the attendees can discuss the most valuable and important Product Backlog items. The Scrum Master facilitates the process, and Developers own the plan.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: The Scrum Team is defining the single objective for the upcoming Sprint. What is this called, and when is it created?
options: The Increment, created during the Retrospective
The Sprint Goal, created during Sprint Planning
The Product Goal, created during the Sprint Review
The Definition of Done, created during the Daily Scrum
items.explanation: The Sprint Goal is the single objective for the Sprint and is created collaboratively during Sprint Planning. It provides focus and is not to be confused with the Product Goal or Definition of Done.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: Mid-Sprint, the Developers discover the work is harder than expected and want to adjust. How should they proceed?
options: Add more hours until the original scope is met
Silently drop the Sprint Goal and wait for the Sprint Review
Collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate scope while keeping the Sprint Goal intact
Abandon the Sprint Goal and start different work
items.explanation: The Sprint Goal should not be compromised; as more is learned, scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner. Abandoning the goal or silently dropping it undermines the Sprint's purpose.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: A Sprint Goal has become obsolete because of a major market change. Who alone may cancel the Sprint?
options: The Scrum Master
The Developers by majority vote
The stakeholders at the Sprint Review
The Product Owner
items.explanation: Only the Product Owner may cancel a Sprint, and cancellation is rare because it is based on whether the Sprint Goal is still viable. The Scrum Team or stakeholders cannot cancel it.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: A Product Owner wants to know the Developers' progress toward the Sprint Goal each day. What is the appropriate event?
options: The Daily Scrum, a fifteen-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress and adapt their plan
A daily status report written by each Developer for the Product Owner
A daily review meeting led by the Product Owner
A daily Sprint Review
items.explanation: The Daily Scrum is a fifteen-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog. It is not a reporting session led by the Product Owner.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: Which description best matches the purpose of the Sprint Review?
options: To check whether the Developers met their individual targets
To inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations, together with stakeholders
To present a formal status report to management
To approve the budget for the next quarter
items.explanation: The Sprint Review is a working session to inspect the Increment and adapt the Product Backlog, involving stakeholders. It is not a status report, budget approval, or individual performance check.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: For a one-month Sprint, what is the timebox for the Sprint Review?
options: A maximum of fifteen minutes
As long as required to cover every backlog item
A maximum of four hours
A maximum of one hour
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide sets the Sprint Review timebox at a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint. Fifteen minutes is the Daily Scrum, and timeboxed events are not open-ended.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: Which event exists to inspect how the last Sprint went and to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness?
options: The Sprint Review
The Daily Scrum
The Sprint Planning
The Sprint Retrospective
items.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is where the Scrum Team inspects individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and the Definition of Done, and identifies improvements. The Sprint Review inspects the product outcome, not the process.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: A Product Owner asks how many Increments can be created within a single Sprint. What is correct?
options: Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint
Exactly one Increment may be created per Sprint
No Increment may be created until the Sprint ends
Only one Increment may be created per release
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide allows multiple Increments within a Sprint; each Increment is additive and must meet the Definition of Done before it can be released.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: The organization has no standard Definition of Done. What should happen?
options: The Scrum Master copies a Definition of Done from another company
The Scrum Team creates a Definition of Done for the product
The Product Owner writes the Definition of Done alone
No Definition of Done is needed in that case
items.explanation: If the organization has no standard, the Scrum Team must create an appropriate Definition of Done. It is a team-owned commitment, not an individual or borrowed document.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: Several Scrum Teams work on one product. What does Scrum require regarding their Definitions of Done?
options: Only the largest team needs a Definition of Done
The Product Owner defines a separate Definition of Done for each team
They must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done
Each team may use a completely different Definition of Done
items.explanation: When multiple Scrum Teams work on the same product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done so their combined work forms a coherent Increment.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: A Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done at the end of the Sprint. What happens to it?
options: It is released and marked as done later
It is permanently removed from the product
It is counted as complete for reporting purposes
It returns to the Product Backlog for rework and reconsideration
items.explanation: Work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not considered Done and returns to the Product Backlog. Releasing it, discarding it, or reporting it complete all misrepresent the product's state.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: Why is a shared Definition of Done important for the Product Owner?
options: It creates transparency about what is truly complete so progress and value are not overstated
It allows the Product Owner to skip the Sprint Review
It replaces the need for a Sprint Goal
It guarantees the product will be defect free
items.explanation: The Definition of Done makes the state of the Increment transparent, preventing overstatement of progress. It does not remove events, replace the Sprint Goal, or guarantee zero defects.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: Which list correctly pairs the three Scrum artifacts with their commitments?
options: Product Backlog with Sprint Goal, Sprint Backlog with Product Goal, Increment with Definition of Done
Product Backlog with Product Goal, Sprint Backlog with Sprint Goal, Increment with Definition of Done
Product Backlog with Definition of Done, Sprint Backlog with Product Goal, Increment with Sprint Goal
Product Backlog with Sprint Goal, Sprint Backlog with Definition of Done, Increment with Product Goal
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide pairs the Product Backlog with the Product Goal, the Sprint Backlog with the Sprint Goal, and the Increment with the Definition of Done.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: Who owns the Sprint Backlog during the Sprint?
options: The Scrum Master
The stakeholders
The Developers
The Product Owner
items.explanation: The Sprint Backlog is owned by the Developers, who update it and adapt their plan as they learn. The Product Owner owns the Product Backlog, not the Sprint Backlog.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: According to the Scrum Guide, what are the components of the Sprint Backlog?
options: The Product Goal, the budget, and the release date
The Definition of Done, the stakeholders, and the risks
The velocity chart, the burn-down chart, and the backlog order
The Sprint Goal, the selected Product Backlog items, and the plan for delivering them
items.explanation: The Sprint Backlog is composed of the Sprint Goal, the set of Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint, and the plan for delivering them. It is not a collection of charts or management fields.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: Which three pillars underpin the empirical process that Scrum is founded on?
options: Transparency, inspection, and adaptation
Planning, execution, and control
Scope, time, and cost
Analysis, design, and testing
items.explanation: Scrum is founded on empiricism, whose three pillars are transparency, inspection, and adaptation. The other three-part lists belong to different paradigms.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: How do the pillars of empiricism relate to one another in Scrum?
options: Transparency alone is sufficient without inspection or adaptation
Transparency enables inspection, and inspection enables adaptation
Adaptation enables transparency, and inspection enables planning
Inspection replaces the need for transparency
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide explains that transparency enables inspection, which in turn enables adaptation. The pillars build on one another and cannot substitute for one another.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: How do the Scrum values support the empirical process?
options: They guarantee the team will meet its forecasts
They are optional suggestions unrelated to Scrum's mechanics
They build the trust and openness that make transparency, inspection, and adaptation possible
They replace the need for the Scrum events
items.explanation: The Scrum values of commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage create the climate of trust that lets transparency, inspection, and adaptation work. They do not replace events or guarantee outcomes.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: What three topics does Sprint Planning address?
options: The budget, the schedule, and the resource plan
The Product Goal, the Product Backlog, and the definition of value
The team's velocity, the burn-down, and the release plan
Why the Sprint is valuable, what can be done, and how the work will be done
items.explanation: Sprint Planning addresses the Why, What, and How of the Sprint through collaboration of the whole Scrum Team. The other lists describe traditional planning artifacts or metrics.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: A Product Owner attends the Daily Scrum and begins directing the Developers' tasks. What is the most appropriate guidance?
options: The Daily Scrum is for the Developers to inspect and adapt, so the Product Owner should not use it to direct the team's work
The Product Owner should lead the Daily Scrum and assign tasks
The Daily Scrum should be replaced by a status meeting led by the Product Owner
The Developers should stop attending so the Product Owner can lead
items.explanation: The Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan. A Product Owner who uses it to direct work undermines self-management.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: A stakeholder asks whether the Product Backlog will ever be complete. What is the correct answer?
options: No, because it should be deleted once development begins
No, because the Product Backlog is emergent and never complete as the product and environment evolve
Yes, because it is complete once all features are listed
Yes, because it should be frozen at the start of the first Sprint
items.explanation: The Product Backlog is an emergent list that evolves as the product and understanding of it grow; it is never complete. Freezing or deleting it contradicts Scrum.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: Who creates the Sprint Backlog?
options: The Scrum Master
The stakeholders together with the Product Owner
The Developers
The Product Owner
items.explanation: The Developers create and own the Sprint Backlog during Sprint Planning and adapt it throughout the Sprint. The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog but does not create the Sprint Backlog.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner

items.domain: Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
items.stem: New market data suggests that a feature the Product Owner previously ranked low is now highly valuable. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Leave the order unchanged to avoid confusing the Developers
Wait until the next annual planning cycle to change any order
Ask the Developers to stop the current Sprint
Reorder the Product Backlog to reflect the new insight
items.explanation: The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog to maximize value, so new evidence should inform reordering. Avoiding change for comfort, waiting a year, or stopping the Sprint inappropriately all fail to adapt.
items.reference: Scrum Guide 2020 / Scrum.org PSPO I subject areas - Scrum Framework as Applied by the Product Owner
